sentences.text: Elena was ten and lived in La Paz, in a small apartment on the seventh floor of a red-brick building that looked out across the whole city, and beyond it to the great snow-covered peak of Illimani.
She had lived at almost four thousand meters above sea level her whole life, and her lungs were used to the thin cold air in a way that mystified visitors.
Her mother was a doctor at a clinic in El Alto.
Her father, Ernesto, was a naturalist who worked for the Bolivian environment ministry.

He spent most of the year traveling to different parts of the country — the Amazonian lowlands to the north, the Chaco to the east, the altiplano to the south — writing careful reports about small things almost nobody else noticed.
Every February, in the middle of the summer rains, when Elena had school holidays and the altiplano was at its strangest, Ernesto took her on one long field trip.
He had taken her to the highland wetlands when she was eight.
He had taken her to a Chilean-border flamingo lake when she was nine.
This year — her tenth year — he had said, quietly, over supper in early January, "This year, mi hija, we go to the Salar."
They drove south for two days.
The road from La Paz to Uyuni ran across the altiplano — a huge high flat table of grassland between the two ranges of the Andes, at three and a half thousand meters.
There were long stretches with nothing on either side but grass, and one or two vicuñas grazing in the distance, and the occasional adobe farmhouse with a tin roof.
Ernesto drove the ministry's old dark green jeep.
Elena sat in the passenger seat with a book she was not really reading and watched the country go past.
In the back of the jeep, wedged carefully between the tent and Ernesto's field bag, was a small hard camera case that Elena had not seen before.
On the second afternoon, she asked what it was.
Ernesto glanced at the mirror.
"My camera," he said.
"An old one.
My father gave it to me when I was twelve.
I have carried it with me on every trip since.
I do not know why exactly.
I never take pictures with it." Elena thought that was very strange.
She did not press.
She had learned that things her father said in that quiet way often came back later, when he was ready.
They stayed the first night in a small hostel in Oruro.
They stayed the second night in a smaller village called Salinas de Garci Mendoza, which sat at the northern edge of the Salar.
Ernesto knew the family who ran the small guesthouse there — he had stayed with them on many trips.
That evening, over a supper of quinoa soup and roasted potatoes, he told Elena about the Salar.
"It is the largest salt flat in the world," he said.
"Ten thousand square kilometers of dry white salt, three meters thick in most places.
It was once, a very long time ago, an enormous salt lake, and it dried up, and the salt stayed.
For most of the year, it is white and dry and cracked into large hexagons.
You could drive across it in any direction."
He drank some coca tea.
"But in the wet season — now, in February — a shallow layer of rain water sits on top of the salt.
Not deep.
Ankle deep.
It cannot drain because the ground under is impermeable.
So the water just sits.
And because it sits perfectly still on a perfectly flat surface, and because the surface is white and reflective, the whole Salar becomes a mirror.
A ten-thousand-square-kilometer mirror.
When you stand on it, the sky is above you and the sky is below you and there is nothing to tell them apart.
That is why we come in February and not in June.
That is what I brought you to see."
They drove out onto the Salar the next morning.
The road ended at the edge of the salt, and then there was no road — just the flat white surface, and the thin water.
Ernesto stopped the jeep just where the water began.
He and Elena climbed out.
Elena did not say anything for a long time.
She had seen pictures.
Everyone had seen pictures.
But she had not understood, from pictures, what it would be.
It was not a lake.
It was not a plain.
It was something else.

The water was perfectly still, only ankle-deep — she could see the salt surface under it, cracked in wide hexagons — and it reflected the enormous pale sky above so exactly that when she looked out, she could not tell where the ground ended and the sky began.
Distant mountains at the edge of the Salar seemed to be floating, doubled, one above and one below.
She took one step onto the water.
Her boot made a small ring of ripples that spread out in silence and dissolved.
Ernesto went back to the jeep.
He opened the small camera case.
He took out the old dark metal camera.
He also took out, from a small pouch inside the case, a yellow and black cardboard box, and from the box a single roll of film.
He walked back to Elena.
He said, "I have been carrying this camera for thirty years and I have never once put a film in it.
My father put a film in it, when he gave it to me, and I finished that film in the first month.
Then I went to the Amazon for the first time.
And I did not put another film in.
And I never have since.
I have carried it, empty, on every trip.
I do not really know why.
Something to do with my father.
Something to do with wanting to keep it ready but not use it.
I have thought about this for many years and I do not have a clean answer."
He held the camera out to her.
"Today I am putting a film in.
I have brought three rolls.
They are for you.
For this week.
You take the pictures.
I will show you how the camera works.
Then it is yours to hold, for the five days we are here." Elena took the camera.
It was heavier than she had thought.
The dark metal was cool.
It smelled faintly of leather and old grease.
She looked up at her father.
She did not know what to say.
